utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. As you can see, only two Judges are present today. Judge Mindua has another obligation and is not able to attend our hearings this week, so that we are sitting only with two Judges pursuant to Rule 15 bis of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Last Thursday I asked the Prosecution to provide us with an update about witnesses, about the length of the Prosecution case. Are you in a position to give us this update, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. I hope to give you some -- some information, and I would ask, as I think we had sent an e-mail around, that orally to allow us to withdraw three witnesses and those are our numbers, number 42, number 95, and number -- excuse me, I'm looking at the wrong sheet. Those are numbers 59, numbers 153, and numbers 195. And number 196 never quite made it onto our list, but just so everyone knows, we don't have any intention with continuing with 196. The other three that I just mentioned, 42, 95, and 39, we are considering drafting 92 quater because in our contact with them they're very emotionally -- have significant medical issues in our -- as far as we can see at this point, and we are in the process of seeing if we can get doctors' reports or notes or material for that, for a 92 quater motion for them. There are also a few witnesses who we are trying to bring on as best we can. People are not quite as willing as they used to be in the past to come, and so it's taking a bit more of an effort. And Mr. Thayer will be providing, in the next day or two, an updated list of witnesses as he spread them out for the months up to the summer break. It should be similar to what you received before but should have some of the latest information on it. So we -- and I've been speaking to Mr. Gajic, trying to get an idea of how much the Defence may take for witnesses like Rick Butler, General Milovanovic, General Obradovic, these senior colleagues of General Tolimir, and while, of course, it's not absolutely clear, it's my understanding that the General will naturally want to have many days with each of those witnesses, and the exact number of days will -- is not clear yet. And I'll be looking at our estimates for days on them as well. It shouldn't be -- shouldn't have to change too much. But aside from those three or four rather significant witnesses, we are, you know, going along at a pretty good pace and expect to keep that pace and hopefully we won't have any gaps. And if we're lucky, we'll finish the Prosecution's case before the summer break if -- hopefully well before. But as I say, if I said anything firm on that, I'm sure I wouldn't be telling the -- you know, it wouldn't be giving you much guidance because it's still a little tricky trying to find out how long all those two or three important witnesses will take. But Mr. Thayer's working on that updated sheet with all the witnesses grouped by week. And I just got a message from one witness we are planning on calling in two weeks, said, no, they can't absolutely be here, not until April, and so that kind of thing is constant. But it's all manageable. So I can give you those firm three are not there. There's three more that it looks like it's -- I can't bring them here just because they can't come here mentally, so we hope to have a 92 quater going. And we're working on the rest. Most -- the majority, of which are willing, will be here, but that's fundamentally the background that I hope gives you some guidance. And you'll get more guidance when you see the updated sheet from Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey, for this update. It's very helpful. However, I have a question. You mentioned three witnesses the Prosecution is withdrawing. Witness 59, 153, and Witness 195. If I'm not mistaken, the last one, Witness 195 is not yet on the 65 ter witness list. That should be clarified, like it is this case with the Witness 196 you mentioned earlier, that he didn't make it on the list at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of those situations. I have a PW number for 195 of 077, but -- oh, yes. There's -- there was a motion to add 15 December, and I'm reminded that there has not yet been a decision on that, so I can't drop that one formally because he's not formally on. So we can say that we don't need a decision on that particular witness, but that one will not be -- will not be an issue. Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, that was one witness the Chamber decided that the application to add him to the 65 ter witness list would be premature because of a lack of clearance, Rule 70 clearance, if I'm not mistaken. So that he is not on the list and there's no room for withdrawal. But on the other hand, we take note of your intention not to call him and the other witness, 196.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, and I also see at the bottom of my note the name Ewa Tabeau who you'll recall has been on our witness list sort of in conjunction with Helge Brunborg; they authored that report together. And as you will recall, General Tolimir in the cross of Dr. Brunborg brought up a book with a list of some names on it that were allegedly on our missing list. And so we have asked Ms. Tabeau to take a look at those names and to do a brief report on it. So it would be our intention, and I've spoken briefly to Mr. Gajic about that, to -- to call her to give the results of that simple review of names. I hope its simple. And that, of course, would open up her to cross-examination on that work and anything else. And I know -- I don't think I was here, but I know from the record that Mr. -- General Tolimir wanted a chance to cross-examine her. So that remains the same. She will be here for cross-examination on her report for both the small issue and the big issue. So I'm not sure where we have -- we haven't managed to put her in yet because her report isn't done, and we, of course, want to get that translated and to the Defence, but it should be very small. It's just a matter of what she finds about these names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. That was an open question. Any other matters to raise? If not, we should call the witness into the courtroom and continue the cross-examination. The witness should be brought in, please. To enable the witness to enter the courtroom, we turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome back to the courtroom. The blinds should be brought up. Please sit down. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies. And the protective measures are still in place for you. Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Peace unto this house. I wish everyone a pleasant day. And may God's will be done in these proceedings. I wish the witness a pleasant stay amongst us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we start, I would like to remind you of some of the statements you made in the summary provided to us by the Prosecution. For instance, at page 10793, in answer to a Prosecutor's question as to what your interpretation of the word "breakthrough" was, you said that breakthrough was something that you used more in the sense of you traversing a certain area rather than engaging in a military operation. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's how I look at the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to remind both speakers to pause between question and answer. Wait a moment with your answer because the interpreters need some time to interpret everything you are saying. That would be very helpful for all of us. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for your guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in your place of residence, was the 28th Division lined up for the purposes of the breakthrough you referred to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a lineup in the sense you mention it, in the military sense, was not there, not to speak of. It was a gathering of individuals who were forming a single-file line. We didn't know if the area to be traversed was going to be mined or not. Besides, the trail was not wide enough to allow for a wider column to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who was it who formed a column in single file or two abreast?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really wouldn't be able to tell you that. It was night-time. I could see people setting out from a large meadow. There was no forming of an orderly line in that sense. People simply went on their way. That's how I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, did all the able-bodied men from Srebrenica set out from your village in the direction of Nezuk on the so-called breakthrough? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part. Some of them, of course, headed toward Potocari, namely women and children. There were also able-bodied men among them. It was down to one's choosing. Of course, in addition to what were mostly women, there were men as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was the column setting out from your village in the direction of Nezuk mostly formed of men from Srebrenica ... mostly formed of soldiers from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that they were soldiers. I know that some of them wore a military uniform. But if they all departed or not, I can't really tell you. There were 15.000 people in all. It was very difficult to make out what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, the Chief of Staff of the Srebrenica Brigade, did he ask that the brigade be lined up and formed a column that was supposed to break through the VRS lines departing from your village in the direction of Nezuk?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered the question. I didn't see anyone specifically lining up individuals. They naturally formed a column, but I didn't see any military units being lined up or anyone who would seem to have taken up the task of leading the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That evening when the column set out toward Nezuk, were there representatives of the civilian authorities of Srebrenica in your village and did they join the column? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me when I tell you that I wasn't aware of any civilian authority in existence at the time. And even if there had been, I don't think it would have been likely for me to be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 10798, in answer to the Prosecutor's question about the existence of the 28th Division and your related statements from Krstic, you said that after the signing of the agreement on demilitarisation there was no military unit. So I'm asking you now: On the 9th and 10th and 11th of August, 1995, did there exist a 28th Division in that area?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did Srebrenica have any sort of army in July of 1995 or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is possible that there were people engaged in the defence exercise. That's quite possible. But there was no army to speak of. There was no commander. And I don't think that there was any general defence effort. I do believe that individual villages that came under attack were defended though. On the other side, where I was -- where I resided at the time was quite on the other side, so I can't really testify to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that there was no commander, do you have anyone specific in mind or did you mean the role itself?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I meant Naser Oric, him in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if Naser Oric had a deputy and, if so, what his name was?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe that he had one, but I don't know his name. I wasn't interested in that. I was out of the system. I was disconnected from it all. We didn't have any means of communicating.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You started explaining about the couriers who came in and passed on the message. Well, should they not have been sent by some sort of an authority, if not by the commander himself then in his absence by his deputy who should be in command of the army?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I truly don't know whether they were sent by anyone. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show in e-court D001, page 4. Thank you. We'll be looking at lines 1 through 7 on page 4 in paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at the last paragraph. You have it on your screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, may I interrupt you for a moment. I think it would be helpful for the witness but also for the Chamber first to see the first page of this document so that we all know what is it about. And then you may move to the relevant pages you want to use with the witness. First the first page in English and B/C/S of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we have page 1 of D001 both in BH and English. Let me tell you that this is a statement by Mr. Ramiz Becirovic given to the 2nd Corps of the Army of the Bosnia-Herzegovina in Tuzla on the 11th of August, 1995. You can see that it states there, "I, Ramiz Becirovic," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does this refresh your memory in any way? Was this Becirovic Naser Oric's deputy?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. He probably was if he gave this statement. I don't know. But I cannot give you my comments on something I'm not sure about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well. He will be speaking to the same events you were speaking to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 4, paragraph 5, which is the last paragraph on that page. It's page 5 in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see the last paragraph. I'll be reading it out. "Once we surrendered our weapons to UNPROFOR, in 1994 and 1995 we received a certain quantity of materiel and technical equipment which was smuggled through the defence lines and the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps. I was told by Kasim Suljic, who is currently serving in the division command in Tuzla, that the transfer of materiel and technical equipment had been carried out in co-operation with the then-commander of the operational group Hasan Muratovic." This is my question: Did you hear anything about the arming of the Muslims in 1994 and 1995, and did you hear anything about the arrival of weapons in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything about this. I am not familiar with this. Had weapons been coming our way, it would certainly have been useful, but I don't believe that was the case. I don't see in what way they would be arming themselves. Where would the weapons be coming from? But I can't tell you anything. I don't have information about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see that the deputy commander, Becirovic, said that it arrived by land from the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have D67 shown. 1D67.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting for it to appear, let me tell you that it's a report submitted to Alija Izetbegovic by Rasim Delic. This is something you'll see on the last page where he signed it. He sent it on the 13th of July, 1995, following the fall of Srebrenica. It was sent through the command of the 1st Corps to the president of the Presidency of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and he details in it what the efforts were that he undertook to arm Srebrenica. Let me quote from beneath the first paragraph. The second line reads: "The General Staff of the army took a number of military actions in order to organise the army members in the enclave and prepare them for possible action." And then in the first bullet point he says: "Specifically the following has been done for Srebrenica and Zepa: Bullet point 1, to start with, lethal assets and materiel and technical equipment were brought in on foot in fairly small quantities." So he confirms what Becirovic said. Second bullet point: "Seventeen helicopter flights were carried out in each of which a helicopter was hit." And in reference to these helicopter flights, he goes on to detail what it was that was brought to Srebrenica and from Srebrenica to Zepa. So now we'll look at specifically these items.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we have page 22 shown in e-court. My apologies, it's page 2. My mistake, I said 22. I apologise to the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And for the record, this is D67 and not 1D67 as indicated earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see a table. On the right-hand side we see it in English. It's in somewhat larger print but you can read the figures. You see that it says 7.62 millimetre rounds, 173.000 were brought into Zepa, 354.000 to Srebrenica. And then, under 2, 7.62 bullets, 4.360 to Zepa and 20.324 for Srebrenica. Next, 7.62 bullets, 54 millimetres. We see that the first column relates to Zepa, the second to Srebrenica, et cetera. Next follow other assets that were sent such as rifle launch grenades, launchers for RPG, et cetera, rockets, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 3 shown in e-court, please. Thank you. On page 3 we see that among the supplies reaching the areas were uniforms and other equipment including anti-aircraft ammunition, under 55, hand-held launchers, snipers, rockets, et cetera. Can we have page 3 shown, to see the signature. That's page 4 in Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: There we see the signature, commander army General Delic. Rasim Delic. Please, did you have any sort of information to the effect that weapons were being sent across Zepa to Srebrenica and that Zepa and Srebrenica were one entity under one military organisation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it well. Had this reached us, indeed, it would have been very good. I think Srebrenica as a location with the population there was forgotten by all, starting with the army commander, forgotten by the UN and Yasushi Akashi. I think we were left to our own devices, and we all know what followed. It's nice what it says on the paper about these things being sent, but I didn't feel any of it coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a possibility that Becirovic, who was the Chief of Staff, and the army commander Rasim Delic falsely reported this data to their president, Mr. Izetbegovic, without having actually delivered the assets?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't answer that. I'm just a regular person who had no insight into what is mentioned therein. I see this for the first time. I really can't comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D126. Thank you. Thank you. We are going to see it shortly. We can see Naser Oric's photograph. And this article is entitled, "Weapons that were handed over were out of order." It was a public article in a newspaper. Since it is not legible, could we please zoom in. Thank you. He says -- and we are looking at the fourth line. Could we please move the text to the left-hand side so that we could see the last column. We still can't see that. It says 3.350 troops. The fourth, the fifth line. Sorry, not the line, the column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please move the original article to the left so that we can see the -- further. Please further. Please move it to the left so that we can see the last column on the right. Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, now it seems to be on the screen, but what are you asking for?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The fifth line underneath the heading or the subheading "Guards Along the Lines," which is page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "We had some 2.000 barrels, I knew that for sure. And I did not know everything. Weapons were being hidden. We kept some 20 cannons, for sure, with four barrels. We made single-barrel cannons out of them, so in the end they were a kind of anti-aircraft cannons. Let me explain. We hid every single piece that we managed to capture from the Chetniks. When we went into action, we would take them with us. Everybody hid weapons from everyone else. Only the real soldiers, the bold ones, reported their weapons. The other ones were hiding them until needed. It is all understandable. We probably had around 4.000 barrels. And it became obvious that it was so during the break-through to Tuzla, leaving aside the brigade in Zepa." Is it Naser Oric speaking about the way weapons were concealed by weapons -- by soldiers so as not to be handed over to UNPROFOR and the rest and that in the end they may have had as many as 4.000 pieces?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on this. It is his statement. I really don't know. I wasn't informed of this. I was at the front lines, then I went to the hospital. And the weapons that there were, were few, and I see some tall figures here. If we had had that, we would not have needed UNPROFOR. We could have defended ourselves. I don't know who wrote this, and I really can't comment on it. I'm not privy to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D001 again, which is Ramiz Becirovic's statement. Let us again go to page 4 where he says the same thing Oric did, in the sense that people hid weapons in their houses. We have it. Is it page 4? The fourth paragraph on that page. It is page 5 in e-court. The fifth line of the fourth paragraph. It begins with the words "It is customary ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "It was customary that soldiers held onto their weapons, and only exceptionally they would hand them over to other soldiers at the front line. It was never allowed that all weapons be grouped in a single location. Heavy weapons had been turned over to UNPROFOR. And as far as I recall, this was handed over: Two tanks, Howitzers, a cannon, et cetera." My question is this: As a soldier, did you know at all that soldiers had their weapons at home; they did not hand them over or take them to the barracks or to any other assembly points?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to be in the TO before 1993. Following that, I wasn't informed of it. As for that number of weapons and that people had those in their homes, I don't think it's correct. What weapons there were prior to 1993 was very little. I don't know about these two tanks. I didn't see them, although they may well have been there. As for the rest, whether people had anything in their homes, that is something I can't say, although I don't think it was likely. There simply weren't so many weapons around for people to keep them at home. And whatever there was, was handed over to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber whether there is a possibility that the Chief of Staff and deputy commander of the Srebrenica division lied to the 2nd Corps of the Army of B&H? Was he telling lies when providing this statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on anyone else's position. I'd be speculating. Whoever said to someone else, that's not for me to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to comment. I'm asking you to tell us what you know, given that the commander said one thing, the Chief of Staff said another thing, and you say a third thing. So different people are telling different things.

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm only telling you what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you asked for a comment, not for his knowledge. You asked whether there is a possibility that the Chief of Staff and deputy commander, and so on and so on, lied to the chief of the 2nd Corps. This is asking for a comment and not of his knowledge. You should indeed focus on the knowledge and the facts the witness can testify about. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, were you a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Srebrenica, and did you have your own weapon at home?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the TO until March or April 1993. I did not have weapons at home. When I went to the front lines, there were some weapons there. I didn't have any at home. We had some weapons provided to us but not many. There were some rifles and the likes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked you a moment ago whether in the column you saw some soldiers with weapons. Do you want me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have in mind the entire column, I think there were people with weapons. As for whether they were soldiers or not, I can't say. They could have been. In any case, there were some light weapons. Those who were in the front may have had some. As for the others who remained behind, they were without weapons and they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say those who managed to get through at the front, how many were there? Because the Chamber needs to have a figure. Do you know how many people there were with how many pieces of weapons and how many remained in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know how many managed to pull through. You probably know as well as I do. I arrived on the 10th day, and they had gone through on the 5th or the 6th. I know some managed to get through. I don't know how many weapons. I can't say. Had I seen them, I probably would have been one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at page 12 of the document. In the English it is page 14, line 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here we see that it is stated as follows: "On the 11th of February, 1995, at the other end of the line, I had the Chief of Staff in the corps. I informed him of the situation in Srebrenica and that it had basically fallen. I also advised him of our intention to go towards Tuzla. He cautioned me about the risks we were taking upon ourselves. My answer to him was that we had no other choice. He wanted me to tell him the general direction which we were to take." It is Ramiz Becirovic's statement. On this page he says he acquainted the Chief of Staff of the corps that they were about to set out from Srebrenica. We'll skip a number of pages and go to line 9, where he says, I quote, line 9 of this statement, just below the passage I've read out: "In the column there were between 10- and 15.000 people. In my estimate there were between 10- and 15.000 people in the column. I had around 6.000 troops, discounting those from Zepa. There weren't many women in the column and I didn't see many children either. Maybe there were about a dozen women." My question for you is this: Were there indeed 6.000 fighters in that column, as the Chief of Staff says?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that many fighters. I didn't see as many. That is certain. You could ask him about that. He mentions the 11th and the 12th of July, 1995. He can say what he wishes, and there's nothing I can comment about. I didn't see as many. Had there been so many, perhaps not so many would have been killed and more would have gotten through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was the column divided into fighting units comprising those 6.000 soldiers, or did the soldiers merge with the civilians?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people moved on their own. I didn't see anyone in command, someone who would be in charge of the column. I didn't see people asking what to do. They just went along. That was it. As for the fighters, it is possible that there were some people in uniform. But as for proper units with equipment and weapons with people heading the column, that didn't exist. I wish it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at line 17 to 21. I quote Mr. Ramiz Becirovic, the Chief of Staff: "As a wounded person, I managed to secure a horse for myself, and I moved as part of the 280th Brigade, which was the second brigade in the column. At the helm was the 274th Brigade -- 284th Brigade because they were familiar with the area and they acted as our reconnaissance. It was a very long column." My question is this: Were you in the first part of the column where the 280th and the 284th Brigade were?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was so. I think I was around the middle of the column. Whether the column was divided by brigades, I don't know. It is true that people from Kamenica and Zvornik were at the front, those who lived closer to Tuzla, because they were more familiar with the terrain, and I heard some people say so. Whether the column was divided in brigades, that's something I don't know. Perhaps he had more information and perhaps that's the way he understood it to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were there any wounded individuals in your part of the column?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we set out in the morning, some of the individuals had to be carried to our first stop, which was the village of Kamenica. When on the 12th the darkness fell at perhaps 8.00 or 9.00 p.m., suddenly we were being shelled. We were being shelled from artillery pieces and came under machine-gun fire. So this was the evening attack in Kamenica which made it impossible to carry the wounded onwards anymore. There were too many of them. I even personally tried to help some of them, but it was impossible to help anyone. There was heavy fire and it was difficult to save your own skin, let alone that of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell Their Honours how many there were, roughly, of the wounded?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to say. It was night-time. We were in a forested area. I came upon the area where most of these people were located. I was looking for my brother and father. There were really many of them, both those who were wounded and those who were killed. I tried to help two or three of them when all of a sudden artillery fire was opened again, or actually, all sorts of weapons engaged. When I came to the identification centre in Tuzla at a later date, I realised that my brother's remains were recovered in that specific area, so he must have been killed there. But it's difficult to tell how many people there were. It was dark. And it wasn't a small number of people that you could easily count. There were many who were killed and wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at line 12 on this page in Serbian. I'm sorry, page 12, line 31, in Serbian. And in English it's line 6 from the bottom where you see 282 somewhere in the line. This is what the commander says: "I placed the wounded right behind the 284th Brigade, while the mountain battalion was supposed to be attached to the rear. That was where the commander of the 282nd Brigade approached me, Ibro Dudic, who had called over the commander of the 281st Brigade, Zulfo Tursunovic, and told he me that I was preparing his murder. I saw that he was fearful. He asked that, from among the elements of the 284th Brigade, his men, the scouts, come back to him who had been reconnoitering the area. I did not permit this. He told me that he had designated around ten young men of whom it was certain that some would cross over to the free territory. He had given them the task of killing me if ever I crossed over." This is my question: Were there any conflicts and confrontations among the commanders and specific units that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's the first time I see this statement and hear this information. I really know nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But did you yourself hear of any internal confrontation and killing?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do know that there were people who went crazy. Was it caused by poison or simply was it shell shock? I knew about that. But I didn't hear and wasn't able to see anyone kill someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what happened to those men who went crazy all of a sudden?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to describe what it was that that they were doing. You never spent more than a second in any given spot or else you would have been killed by the fire. You would see a person and then you would never see him again. We didn't have an area where we would meet and be able to discuss what we would be doing next. I suppose such individuals wandered around until they came across VRS soldiers who killed them, and that's probably how most of them met their end.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at line 9 from the bottom of the page. In English it's the next page. We have the next page now, and let me quote line 56: "I stopped the column from moving with a Motorola." That's what Mr. Becirovic says. Did you feel that there were commanders of the BH Army relaying orders given to them over a Motorola?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there were, but it would have been good had there been some. I think I saw only one individual carrying a Motorola, and that was from far off. It happened above Kamenica on a hill that I just referred to a moment ago. He was not able to contact anyone because what we kept hearing was the Serbian side saying that it would be good if we surrendered as such and such a time on the following day. Who it was who had this Motorola, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 57 in Serbian. That's line 7 from the top or, rather, line 9 from the top. Page 12, line 56. I apologise. It's the 8th or 9th line from the bottom. In English, it's the page we have on our screens, i.e., page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: This situation referred to by Becirovic, is it consistent with what you've just described? And I'll quote this: "I tried to get in touch with the commander of the 282nd Brigade and 283rd Brigade as well as with the battalion, but I wasn't able to get hold of anyone, and the Chetniks jammed our communication. Some ten minutes later, I managed to get hold of a battalion commander who told me that he was on the move heading toward our objective. Since I knew that he was at the rear, I thought that the column had been re-established. I received a request from the commander of the 284th Brigade to go to the head of the column." So I repeat my question: This sort of situation with people being able to establish communication within the column, is that consistent with your memory of these events?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you everything I know. I can't tell you if he really did what he's describing here as having done. I can only talk about my personal experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's read from page 13 of this statement in Serbian, which will most likely be page 15 in English. It's the page we have in English, and it's at the very bottom of the page. This is what Mr. Becirovic had to say in line 27: "There upon, I changed my mind and I placed the mountain battalion and the sabotage company on the elevation with 20 men from the 284th Brigade who were familiar with the area. They were tasked with collecting men in the area of Draca and they were to return on that evening and try to pull out the rest of the column. We headed from Drc in the Losa [phoen] village" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear at what time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you in this section of the column, and do you recognise any of what is being described here as having happened there?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot comment on this individual's statement. I don't think things happened this way. I don't think this has been realistically described. People were being caught and killed as animals on the way. Had things proceeded this way, then everything would have been fine. I don't know what his intention is in making these comments. I know that there was no army out in the field that was able to protect individuals. Individuals were being taken prisoner in large numbers, 1.000, 2.000, and they were taken away and shot until one by one all of them were exterminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say now they were killed; you didn't say that at the time. At any rate, let me show you something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at page 13 of this statement, will which will be line 10 from the bottom. That's line 54 from the top. In English that's page 16, line 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where, in line 53, Mr. Becirovic says: "Sometime at 1200 hours on the 15th of July, 1995." It's in the middle of the page in English, you can see it. Do you see the bit where it says "15 July"?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "I received information that the commander of the 284th Brigade and battalion commander Ejub Golic had been wounded, and I was told that they doubted that Golic would survive. We made a line opposite Baljkovica, and the main body of our section of the column also set off later on. That evening we started fighting in order to break through toward the free territory. In the fighting, we destroyed three self-propelled guns. We captured three tanks. We destroyed a tank in the morning as it was moving toward Baljkovica. We destroyed two trucks and a Praga, capturing one. After night fall, we stopped fighting in order to resume in the morning. Since we could only engage one tank in the fighting, as we were moving along, we set fire to the fuel tanks because there was no other way for us to destroy them. Simultaneously with our attack, an attack was launched from the direction of free territory, which was" - and here we have to turn to the next page - "led by commander Naser Oric. But they were unable to break through the Chetnik defence line on that day. That morning, they launched yet another attack from the direction of Nezuk and acting in co-ordination with our forces succeeded in linking up at around 1200 hours when I met Naser. Our forces were crossing over that line, pulling out over a period of several days in small groups," et cetera, end of quote. As you got out to Nezuk, did you hear anything of the breakthrough at Baljkovica where you were captured?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you seem to be insisting on questions I cannot help you with at all. I can tell Their Honours what it was that I personally experienced. This isn't something I can comment on. You are probably better placed to comment on it than I am. I don't think it useful for me to tell you what it was that I heard from others. It's not pertinent to my answer. I can't give you an answer. I really don't know if things happened this way or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, was this something that could be described as a passage or as a breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm no expert on this score. I'm just an ordinary individual. I can call it passage or breakthrough, regardless. It's up to you to use the term you deem useful. I know that people passed through that area. We all do. Now, if they crossed the territory in the way described here or not, I don't know. I spent every minute of my life there trying to stay alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll be now watching a video of this passage, as you call it. Since you weren't there, let's look at this together. That's why I asked you if you had heard anything about it from anyone. This is D15. The column coming out of the VRS-controlled territory into Nezuk. This is the part of the story just referred to by Mr. Becirovic, where he and Mr. Oric fought their way across the VRS defence lines.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We were able to see this part of the footage featuring men coming out toward Nezuk. Can you tell if these individuals are wearing uniforms and weapons?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to this footage here? Well, yes, I can see it full well. I can see that they do have uniforms, weapons, everything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you can see it for a few more seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have D176 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting for it, I can tell you that it's an ABiH document. It's 2nd Corps of the 27th of July, 1995. The title is "Chronology of Events Surrounding the Breakthrough by the 28th Division." Personally to commander Rasim Delic. We have a full chronology of the events in question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The seventh and eighth bullet point, I quote: "From the 21st and the 25th Division of the land forces, one company from each was sent to Srebrenica to be engaged in fighting there. Following the orders of the 2nd Corps," the number of which we can see here, "of the 9th of July, 1995." The next bullet point: "Order by the 25th division of the land army for all units to be ready to be engaged in the breakthrough towards Srebrenica." These are all orders issued on the 9th. And then we see those of the 10th of July, 1995, since this is a chronological sequence. My question is this: Did you have any knowledge of three land army divisions of the 2nd Corps taking part in the breakthrough in order to establish a corridor at Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they were there. And I'm quite upset for them not being there. They should have helped the people. You indicated here that some people did manage to pull through and you probably think that they too should have been killed. Had things been done properly, they should have provided people to assist those coming out. And I'm quite upset with the whole situation. I believe the people in question were betrayed by all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to page 5 of the document. Paragraph 11. Actually, bullet point 11, which is the third from the bottom. You can see it. The second from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It reads: "At 4.30 on the 16th of July, offensive operations of joint units of the 24th Division and the aforementioned units of the 2nd Corps began in the wider area of Baljkovica. During the afternoon, the aggressor lines were broken through along a perimeter of 2 kilometres. In the general area of Baljkovica, a corridor was set up." And they provide the exact location of the corridor in the document. My question for you is this: Was there indeed a breakthrough or a passage of military conscripts from Nezuk across RS territory?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I see this for the first time, and I'm really not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to page 6 of the document next. The first paragraph on that page. We can see it now. We will find it in the English, I believe, as well. The next page in the English, please. I apologise. It seems we have to go a page back because what I'm look for is at the bottom of the previous page in the English. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says here: "During combat operations, units of the 28th Division and the 24th Division of the land forces, the aggressor suffered significant losses. Twenty bodies of enemy soldiers remained behind in our territory. And according to enemy reports intercepted by the PEB, they took 30 bodies back to the hospital in Zvornik. Six enemy soldiers were captured and a self-propelled gun as well as a tank, which were immediately introduced in combat against the aggressor. Another self-propelled gun and an ammunition depot were set on fire in the village of Baljkovici." During the passage or the breakthrough, should one expect that there are going to be victims exceeding by far the number specified by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not up to me to comment. But since you insist, I'll tell you this: If you walk down the street and come under an attack, are you supposed to not to defend yourself or, if you do, are you automatically to blame for anything? If you are alive walking down the street, it's normal that you will react. At least you would run. If these people were attacked, of course they had to defend themselves. And in the course of doing so, there may have been some casualties, some victims. I don't know the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we are listening very carefully and we have to note that you are reading long passages of several documents. Most of the answers of the witness were "I don't know," "I have no knowledge about that," "I can't testify about this," "I see this for the first time." The way you are conducting your cross-examination is extremely time consuming and I form the impression that you can't get a statement from the witness in relation to the contents of such a document. He made it clear that he is not the right person to do that. Again you should please consider if this is in your case a good conduct of your cross-examination. It's very time consuming.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for this caution. Could we please have 1D609. Thank you. Thank you. This is a manual on the Laws of War for the armed forces. Could we please go to page 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see paragraph 56, where it says: "Civilians within a military target. Geneva Convention which states: A military target remains a military target even when civilians are found within its confines. Civilians within such a target or in its immediate environment are exposed to the same danger that the target is threatened with." If some civilians were part of -- if some soldiers were part of the column, did they expose the civilians within the column to the same danger the soldiers were in?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, do you believe that those people who went to Potocari and surrendered stayed alive? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer your questions. I'm asking you to answer mine. If there are civilians inside a military column, are they also considered a military target exposed to the same kind of danger?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't comment. I really don't know what you mean when you say a military target. We're talking about people who are trying to save their lives, to stay alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you were at the starting point from which the column set off, can you tell us whether on the 11th in the evening there were people gathering in the place where you lived, people from surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you spend the night there?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR unit which you mentioned that had been there the previous day, some 3- or 500 metres away, did they remain there as well?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think they left that evening. They went back to the UNPROFOR base in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether anyone from UNPROFOR arrived in your village during the night between the 10th and the 11th, and did you have any contact with the representatives of either the army or civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you know that General Mladic offered a cease-fire which was to last until 9.00 a.m. the next day and that he told those representatives negotiating with him to inform the armed forces to lay down their weapons? Was this conveyed to you?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear any such thing and I didn't feel that there was any cease-fire. There was firing going on non-stop as well as shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I wanted to show you a footage indicating that, but my Legal Assistant is telling me that it is actually time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is indeed the case. Just for the record, the last document we have on the screen, it's now D180 MFI pending translation. It's the same at 1D609. We must have our first break now and resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please carry on your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just one matter very briefly. The last document that was displayed on the screen, D00180, that's the exhibit number. And that exhibit was MFI'd through Edward Joseph. And there -- the page that was displayed to this witness had some handwritten markings on it, and for the record it may be useful to know who made those hand markings on the document and in what context they were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. President, the markings do not represent anything significant. We weren't the ones to have made them. It's the ICRC that authored the document, and evidently it was the previous holder of the document who underlined certain points and only wrote "that" in English. And this isn't something that could serve as any additional information to anyone including the witness. Unfortunately, we weren't able to get hold of a clean copy of the book that would have been in immaculate condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I saw in the transcript and I heard that this person "only wrote 'that' in English," but I don't think that this is English what we are looking at on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think I mentioned the English language anywhere. What is written next to the three paragraph reads "Ovo" in B/C/S, or, translated into English, "that."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or "this."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That clarifies the situation. It was a translation issue. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My last question for the witness was whether anyone came in the evening to tell them what sort of message Mladic wanted to convey, and the answer to the -- that the witness gave was in the negative. We have our footage now from 1:40 to 1:48:50 which will show that he did ask that such a message be passed on at every single meeting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the video. It's 1:47:50 to 1:48:50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The video should have a P or D number as well. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P1008. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It's P991. I was wrong about the number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: Was this message by General Mladic given to the army or to you, that once weapons are surrendered, everyone can go to the place of their choosing?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was watching this footage, but I don't know about what you're saying. Was this really something that he said. It would have been good had he honoured what was said. I did see those women and children at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we see all those present at this meeting? These were negotiations between General Mladic and Colonel Karremans and representatives of the Muslim authority, Nesib Mandzic. You'll have a look and see if you can recognise them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. You were able to see these individuals representing the civilians introduce themselves at this meeting with General Mladic. You can see Colonel Karremans there marked by the cursor opposite Mr. Mladic. Thank you. I'd like to move on to document P1174. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you were showing a part of the video and -- but you didn't put any question in relation to that video to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I asked the witness before looking at the footage whether soldiers were conveyed General Mladic's request that the message be conveyed to everyone that they can all go to the place of their choosing. I can repeat the question and the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My question is: What was the purpose of showing this video if you'll not put a question to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, I first put the question and then I showed the relevant footage to the witness to -- in order for him to see that General Mladic did raise this issue. If you so wish, we can go through the process again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, I don't wish anything. I just wanted to help you. If you put this video to the witness, it must have a purpose. Now he has seen it, and what for? What was it for? First you put a question, you received an answer, and then you put the video to him. It's not necessary to continue on that. I just wanted to help you to conduct your cross-examination in a proper way. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I can put the question to the witness again. Evidently it wasn't entered in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did any of the members of the leadership tell you that those who surrender weapons can go wherever they want to, that this was the position expressed by General Mladic at the meeting with the Muslim delegation led by Nesib Mandzic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't heard of anything of the sort. I hadn't heard of any of these individuals before. I may have seen the man somewhere before, but I don't know the lady. I don't know what to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. We have your statement before us. A moment ago you said that we should discuss losses. Let's go through your statement briefly in the little time we have left. Let's look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at line 18 of the second paragraph. We have the relevant page on our screens in both languages, and I'll be quoting your words. Let's start from line 18: "At a time when we were forming a column as we were preparing to leave in the evening at around 2100 hours, a heavy fire was opened from Sandici targeting the gathered civilians. From the Praga's, three-barrelled cannons, anti-aircraft machine-guns, and anti-aircraft cannons and Bofors; while from the opposite direction, that is, the areas of Kravica and Rogac, we were targeted by a tank. The attack lasted a full 30 minutes. As I was lying in the ferns, I heard helpless cries and screams of people who were calling for help amid general panic. As I got up, I saw around me hundreds of dead mutilated bodies as well as individuals who were seriously or slightly wounded." Can you tell us how many people were killed in this location, how many were wounded, et cetera? You can say whatever you wish to say. You wanted to speak about the losses.

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. A moment ago it was this very incident that I was referring to. It says here we were lining up. Well, it doesn't really matter if we were lining up or if we were resting. At any rate, there was a large gathering of people there and there ensued an attack. It happened just the way it was described here. It lasted 30 minutes, but it was a very fierce attack which continued, though admittedly not as heavy as it was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many people were affected by this? What were the losses, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many casualties. But since it was night-time and in a forested area, it was difficult to tell. At any rate, the number of those wounded and killed was high.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us if the fire had been opened from an area close by or from further off? What was the distance?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the shells continued to land and tanks continued firing. The locations involved were the ones that I mentioned. There was also small-arms fire which was probably from closer range. But I don't know what else to tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you've just described this for us, can you tell us if this same event was described by another witness, and I'll read to you what he had to say and you'll tell us what the exact location and other parameters were. The witness says: "We went toward Bobojanske [phoen] Stijene where we linked up with elements of the first group. However, we were surrounded by the Chetniks who opened fire on us. As a result there were over 300 killed and many wounded. We were in complete disarray because both soldiers and civilians fled for their lives. I, together with a group of some ten others," and he is referring to names which I won't mention, "went on my way." So can you tell us, is this the same location that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to comment on other people's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Stop. Please wait a moment with your answer. First no overlap, please. And secondly, I would like to know what is your reference for this quotation. I would like to know from what document you were reading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I was reading from a statement of a protected witness. That was the reason why I didn't want to mention his particulars. It's D151, page 2, paragraph 3. So can we please not broadcast page 1 in order to conceal the identity of the witness. We can only -- we can turn to page 2 and paragraph 3 right away, and you'll see that it was from line 4 through to the end of the paragraph that I quoted from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now, if you recall the question, sir, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not certain whether I can comment on somebody else's statement. I don't know whether he saw 300 people or not. I saw a lot of people. I believe there must have been firing and that they are surrounded. There was shooting all over the place but that's all I know. As for whether he continued with other ten people, that is something I don't know. It's somebody else's statement. I already told you what I know, and this is what I stand by.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I asked you for an approximate number, and you didn't. That is why I offered the statement of another person who also mentions a figure. On page 2 you say that you returned to the spot. Let's look at the second page, paragraph 1, line 5. This is your statement. Let's look at other page. It is P1774.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: P1174.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is the statement we have on the screen. Could we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I need a clarification. Is it P1174?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, P1174. The second page, if possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see it here, the fifth line on that page. You say the following: "Passing along that axis, again I saw many massacred bodies. I couldn't recognise them. I also heard cries of many wounded people asking for help." That is why I asked you that, since you seemed to have visited the location twice. A moment ago you said that you were looking for someone. Since you were doing that, could you guess at the number of those killed?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't see. It was a large number of people and it was dark. I can only presume but I don't think it constitutes evidence. As for the part you are referring to, it wasn't at 9.00, because in your first question you asked me about 9.00, but this was probably at around 12.00 or 2.00 or 3.00. It is correct that I left the location and then went back. Throughout that time, there was a lot of firing and people kept dying and trying to move along. You just couldn't stay in a single place otherwise you would get killed. So you could go forward some 500 metres and go back. And in that stretch you could see how many there were who were killed. And I could see what was going on around me. But as for the entire area, it was impossible to see it all. The whole thing went on the whole night. The next day I saw from a nearby hill that around 1.000 people were taken away from that place to Kravica, to the warehouse where they were killed, including my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: From the location where you were, could you see the warehouse in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you see the column heading that way?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't there. I didn't see it. I saw the column leaving the location in the direction of Kravica which was the next day on the 13th around 9.00 or 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you discuss that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps only very briefly. I don't remember the investigators insisting on it because I wasn't personally involved and they weren't too interested in knowing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On the first page you said hundreds of those who were killed. That's why I quoted another witness who mentioned 300. When you say "hundreds of those killed," do you mean more than 200? Because the Chamber needs facts.

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think several hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But can you tell us 2-, 3-, 400?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, anything I say might be incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That is why I put the other witness's statement to you, trying to get at some facts. Let us go back to your statement at this page. Let's look at line 12. There you say: "Going down towards the village of Kamenica at a pass we encountered a Chetnik ambush. Some 20 to 30 men were killed on that occasion." That is what you say in line 14. Now, you also say that you didn't know them. Tell us this, please: Were those men killed as you came along or had they been killed prior to you arriving there?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were killed at the moment I approached the area. We carried a wounded person, my brother-in-law and I, and fire was opened some 20 metres ahead of us. I think it was from a machine-gun. All those who were there ahead of us were killed basically and I think at least 20 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it close to a graveyard or a cemetery in Kamenica? Because some other witnesses describe similar events.

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't too far from the graveyard but not at the graveyard itself. Say, some 200 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to line 22. There you say: "Late in the evening on the 12th of July, 1995, passing by the local cemetery in Kamenica, we saw about 20 [as interpreted] dead men who had probably been killed because they came upon a mine in a minefield. En route from Kamenica to Konjevic Polje, we came upon many killed and wounded people, but we were unable to assist them in any way. I believe that along that stretch of the route there were around 250 [as interpreted] civilians who were killed or wounded, and I don't know what their names were." The first group of 20 to 30 men at Kamenica, can you tell us whether they were killed in a different location to the other group?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I described that correctly. After the group of 20 was killed, I went to the left some 100 metres. I tried to bypass that area because I concluded there must have been an ambush. I arrived at the graveyard you mentioned. As for the mines, I mentioned that because in front of us, some 20, 30, or 50 metres ahead, I saw two or three or several people who were moving ahead of us. It was dark, and I saw that mines detonated in different locations in three or four places, which was an indication to me that these must have been mines connected with each other. That is why I mentioned land-mines. Continuing some 2 or 3 kilometres further, I saw the people I described. You could simply come upon people who were killed or wounded. The whole route was shelled and fired at.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at lines 33 to 36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just so that the record accurately reflects what's in the statement, the statement provides that "there were close to 150 dead and seriously wounded civilians." Where I think the transcript says 250. Well, in the question that General Tolimir put to the witness, I believe he put to the witness that there were 250.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is page 42, line 9. There's a number "around 250 civilians were killed" mentioned. Thank you. Would you agree with that, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think I said 150. I don't know how it was interpreted. I was reading the statement of the witness. I probably didn't say 250 if it says 150.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have it clear on the record. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's go to line 37 where you say the following: "As we were resting in the woods nearby" -- sorry, line 34. My mistake. "While we rested waiting for nightfall, I watched one of the wounded whom I didn't know activate a hand-grenade called 'kasikara' and press it to his chest. He died instantly." Does this tell us anything about the people who committed suicide because they were under the influence of something? And I believe you also said that some of them withdrew chaotically.

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I could see that. It was on the 13th in the morning. It was en route between Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba. It wasn't exactly on the road itself but a bit further away. I don't think there was anything wrong with him mentally, but he realised that he was seriously wounded and that there was no one who could help him. There was no one there to bandage him or carry him. That's why he chose to kill himself. I mentioned only one such case. I didn't say that all of them killed themselves, but it sounds logical to me that if that person was wounded and couldn't move on, he chose to kill himself. Here I simply referred to the one person I saw do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next have page 3. Page 3, please, the first paragraph, line 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: There you seem to already have reached the region of Baljkovica. You say: "We reached Baljkovica on the 18th of July, 1995, in the morning. We remained there throughout the day." My question is this: In Baljkovica, did you enter any area of defence of a particular VRS unit or were you in an area which was not defended by any unit of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we were in the large area which the VRS could not or was not able to cover. I simply didn't see them. Had I seen them, it probably would have been the end for me. I don't know exactly because I'm not familiar with the terrain there. I simply put this in the context of a general area surrounding Baljkovica, but I don't know how large that chunk is exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If this was outside the combat area, how were you captured then?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't captured on the 18th. We were captured on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it also in the area of Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. But I believe we have come too close to the separation line. I think it was closer at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it tell you then that it was close to the front lines of both sides?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one can't say that you were closer to the front lines of both sides if we were coming from one side, so probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm thinking about your location. If you were close to the separation line, it must mean that you were close to the lines manned by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they were close. One could see it from a hill, but it wasn't close.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Later you say that having survived the execution, which is on page 5, that at around 300 hours on the 20th of July, 1995, you crossed over to the free territory. This is found in lines 6 and 7 of your statement on the last, fifth page. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was 3.00. It must have been 6.00 or 7.00 in the morning. That is when I reached the free territory. If you mean that at 3.00 I had crossed the Serb lines, then that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, you say so. You say that you got through the lines around 3.00. Do you see your statement? It says here: "After a short rest, I managed to get through the Chetnik defence line. And around 300 hours on the 20th of July, 1995, I crossed to the free territory in the area of Nezuk." Is this your statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement certainly is mine. Yes, around 3.00. But between the lines there was still an area which had to be crossed. That is why I say that I arrived in Nezuk at around 6.00 or 7.00 in the morning. This tallies. At 3.00 in the morning I crossed the Serb defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement provided to the Prosecution, which is 1D674, on the last page you said that you arrived at around 6.00 or 7.00. You arrived in the free territory, not in Nezuk. That was on July 20 at around 6.00 or 7.00. Is this the difference you're mentioning, and is this the reason why there is that difference between the statements?

utterances.speaker: PW-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it tallies completely. As far as I know, Nezuk was by -- some 500 metres from the separation line at the most. When I crossed into the free territory, Nezuk was there, so I don't think it took me any longer to reach Nezuk eventually. The rest is completely all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for coming here and testifying. I'd like to thank you on behalf of the Defence, and I wish you a safe journey back. May God bless you. Mr. President, Defence has no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Nevertheless, I would like to clarify the number of the last document you have mentioned in page 46, line 10.
