You said 1D674, the statement to the OTP of this witness. The statement was P1174. Or are you referring to another document? I would like to clarify that for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Precisely. First I referred to P1174 while putting questions to the witness, then I moved on to the other statement he gave to OTP investigators. The first statement was provided to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The second one is 1D674, the statement given to the OTP. I would like to ask that both be tendered into evidence if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The first one is already an exhibit, and the second one I don't find in the list of documents to be used with this witness. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the statement is 1D614 instead of 674. May this be corrected, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: In relation to that document which General Tolimir referred to, he made a reference to the last page. And I don't quite see the statement that he referred to. If he can just give us a little bit more direction as to where that is, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We haven't had it on the screen at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct. I'm just ensuring that what was referenced from the witness's statement was in fact derived from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be helpful. Although you completed your cross-examination, we should have it on the screen and to familiarise ourselves with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if it may not be broadcast, as it identifies the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. It will not be broadcast. We should have 1D614 on the screen. That is coming. Sir, do you recall having seen this and signed this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did see it, and I did sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we go to the last page. I think the previous page. Mr. Tolimir, which paragraph was the relevant paragraph you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The relevant portion was paragraph 3, the last three lines: "This happened on Baljkovica mount overlooking Nezuk. I managed to get on my feet, and I arrived the next day on 20 July between 6.00 and 7.00 in the morning on the free territory." Let me highlight for the record that this statement was referred to yesterday when we spoke about those two soldiers who arrived to pass information to the civilian population in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, do you want to comment on that again, this part of your statement to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I did say that things happened the way they are described herein, that it was between 6.00 and 7.00 in the morning that I arrived onto free territory. I crossed the Republika Srpska defence line sometime around 3.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document 1D614 will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D181 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Hasan, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I have no questions on re-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your testimony here in this trial. Thank you very much that you were able to come to The Hague and to testify here and to help us to consider the facts and find out the truth. Thank you very much again, and now you are free to return to your normal activities. And the Court Usher will assist you. Thank you again. We turn for a short moment into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the usher please open the screens. Good afternoon, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, Your Honour Judge Nyambe. Good afternoon, everyone. There is a matter that we need to dispose of before the -- well, before the next witness is brought in, and that refers to her report from January 2010. This was the subject of a 94 bis application of the Prosecution some time ago. And I raised this matter with Mr. Gajic a few weeks ago in anticipation of her evidence. And I also was in contact with the Chambers with respect to the disposition of this issue and was instructed that an oral application to add the application would be appropriate. With that in mind, Mr. President, I do move to add Dr. Barr's, I believe it's 8 January 2010 report. And let me see if I have a number to identify it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 7212.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you very much, Mr. President. It is 8 January 2010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But that not the only document you have listed which are not yet on the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That is correct. There are the photographs that actually are part of that report, part of the analysis that was conducted, that came to my attention when I spoke to Dr. Barr, I think it was on the 1st of March, and she provided those photographs to us. I disclosed them, obviously, to Mr. Gajic in anticipation of the report. So it's part of it because they are specifically referenced as part of the microscopic examination of the document she considered, but they weren't appended to the report so to speak. So I would also offer that in, together with the report. It's 7212A 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what about the three other reports, 65 ter 2858, 2859, and 2860?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I believe that those reports were a part of the application that we made in November 2009 which was decided by the Trial Chamber and the decision which covered 92 bis and 94 bis applications, because Dr. Barr was one of the witnesses that the Prosecution proposed on both the basis of 92 bis and also tendered 94 bis reports for her. And I believe that decision actually disposed of all of the applications with respect to experts that also fell under 92 -- fell under 92 bis as well as 94 bis. And the resolution of it, I believe, was to admit them but to have the expert appear for cross-examination. That's my best recollection of it. And I believe that Dr. Barr was specifically referenced in that as witness number 9, as opposed to Dr. Brunborg who was also the subject of that same issue, who was witness number 15. So I think that they are provisionally admitted. If I'm mistaken, then I would obviously make that motion. But I believe that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't think that this is the case otherwise you would have used the P numbers. But on the other hand, these three are, in my understanding, not yet on the 65 ter be exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand that they actually are on the 65 ter exhibit list. I suppose, rather than belabour the issue, I can probably sort this out at some point during the break. I do intend to use them though, I have to say, with Dr. Barr, but I would propose perhaps using them in a somewhat limited way until we resolve the issue definitively so that we can perhaps proceed with her testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What is the position of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just as Mr. Vanderpuye said, we were in contact with the OTP and with Court Officers in relation to the report by Dr. Barr. If I remember correctly, they were the subject of two 94 bis filings which are still outstanding. The documents were disclosed in a timely fashion in the period indicated by the Prosecution, and the Defence also filed its response under 94 bis. In that response, the Defence expressed its wish to cross-examine the witness on the contents of these reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is the reason why the witness is here. And the Defence has, of course, the opportunity to cross-examine the witness. I don't see an objection to add these documents to the 65 ter exhibit list. That seems to be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave to add these documents to the 65 ter exhibit list is granted. If there are no other matters to discuss before the witness enters the courtroom, then the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Barr. Welcome to the courtroom. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mr. Vanderpuye has some questions for you during his examination-in-chief. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you again, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, Dr. Barr. Because you and I speak the same language, I'm going to ask you to try to speak a little more slowly than you would otherwise to give the interpreters an opportunity to catch up with us and translate accurately what we say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And in particular, please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, do you recall having testified in the case of Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic on the 25th and 26th of June, 2007?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review the entirety of that testimony before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And having reviewed your testimony, does it fairly and accurately reflect what you would say were you to be examined here today and asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would move to admit Dr. Barr's prior testimony, which is P1182, which is the under seal version, and P1183.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Both the documents will be received as exhibits with these numbers, the first one under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In addition, Mr. President, I would move to admit the associated exhibits that were admitted through Dr. Barr in her prior testimony and that would be all of the exhibits listed under the second category with the exception of P1124.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I saw you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right. I saw something that I misunderstood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The documents P1184 through P1192 with the exception of P1124 will be received as exhibits. I think P1124 is already an exhibit. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do have a brief summary of Dr. Barr's prior testimony which I'd like to read into the record. And then I have a number of questions for her. Dr. Barr is a professional forensic document examiner. She holds a Ph.D. in plant pathology which she obtained in 1992 and is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down while reading, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is a member of the council for the registration of forensic practitioners, an accredited agency. She has since worked in forensic document analysis, carrying out handwriting signature comparisons as well as other analyses. First for the Metropolitan Police Forensic Science Laboratory, where she remained until 1999. And thereafter for a private firm, Forensic Document Analysis Limited. Throughout her career, Dr. Barr has performed many thousands of handwriting comparisons related to various issues, including confessions, mortgages, wills, and other legal documents, as well as fraud-related matters. She analyses signatures as a means of identification, as well as groups of documents (so as to identify documents produced by one person). Forensic examiners also typically conduct examinations relating to typewriters, printers, counterfeit documents, indented impressions, alterations, and obliterations. Dr. Barr has given evidence in court concerning her work on approximately 50 occasions as well as before this Tribunal. During her testimony, Dr. Barr explained the process of handwriting analysis and the role of a forensic handwriting expert in determining the extent and the manner in which similarities or differences presented in discrete writings can be of significance. She explained the conclusions reached with respect to these analyses are expressed in terms of a range of opinion from conclusive evidence either showing identity or excluding identity, with inconclusive evidence representing the middle point in the continuum. Per the practice of Dr. Barr's firm, all conclusions are subject to a peer review process. Dr. Barr testified about five reports she produced at the request of the Office of the Prosecutor. These concern certain entries made in the Zvornik Brigade duty operation's officer log-book and the brigade's forward command post or IKM log-book. Dr. Barr was able to find strong evidence of identity for entries made by several members of the Zvornik Brigade. In particular, Dr. Barr concluded, inter alia, that there was strong evidence that Zvornik Brigade chief of engineering, Major Dragan Jokic, made several entries in the duty officer's log-book. She elaborated upon this analysis in a subsequent report. Dr. Barr further found that Zvornik Brigade chief of security, Drago Nikolic, produced entries in the Zvornik Brigade IKM log-book as well as in the duty officer log-book for 15 July 1995. Dr. Barr noted that while she does not understand B/C/S, such an understanding is not necessary to undertaking a handwriting comparison involving the language, as the important analytical element is the manner in which characters are constructed. As such, she has been able, successfully, to analyse handwriting in B/C/S, as well as in other languages using Roman language characters. Mr. President, that concludes my brief summary. And I do have a number of questions I'd like to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, are you still employed with Document Evidence Limited?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No. We sold the company to another forensic company in 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you currently engaged in the same kind of work --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- that you were doing there.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And to date, how long have you been engaged in forensic document analysis?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Since 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Just about 19 years?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in the context of your current work, does your firm employ any new methodologies or protocols that is different now than it was at the time that you last testified?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No. We do exactly the same, use exactly the same procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does your firm now use equipment or instrumentation that is different than it was when you last testified in 2007, and does that -- if so, does that affect any of the prior conclusions that you've reached?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No. We have exactly the same equipment that we had prior to 2007, and it wouldn't affect any of the opinions that I reached in those earlier reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Has there been any change in the way that the peer review process or the review process in general takes place now than it did back then?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No, there hasn't been any changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, I know that you've produced a number of reports since you last testified, which I'd like to get into in some detail a little bit further on, but I'd just like you to familiarise the Trial Chamber, if you could, just with the fundamentals of forensic document analysis as regards handwriting in particular.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: In order to compare handwriting, the most important fact is the word that it's a comparison. So what we would normally do is we have writing that's in dispute or questioned and we have specimen writing that we want compared with the questioned writing. In order to undertake that comparison, we take a systematic process of going through all the letters of the alphabet, A through to Z, and all the numbers, and determining how the pen has moved across the paper to form the construction of those characters, and also to work out the range of variation, because obviously human beings aren't robots; they don't reproduce things in exactly the same way every single time, but they conform to a range. So we assess the range. And we also look at other factors of the handwriting, for example, the quality, how fluently it's been written, how characters are joined to other characters, the slant, the size, the overall proportions, how high things ascend or descend below lines, to get an overall feel for each letter. We do that for the specimen writing, we do exactly the same thing for the questioned writing, and we then compare the two to determine how those ranges overlap, if they do, and the significance of any similarities or differences that we might find. So, for example, a simple letter I is normally written just as a vertical line, possibly with a dot above it. You would expect to find similarities in two people's writings. It wouldn't necessarily be significant because it's a very simple construction, so you have to be able to assess the significance of any similarities or differences. For example, some people might use different constructions depending where in a word a letter was. So, again, you might see differences that wouldn't necessarily be indicative of different writers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask, in terms of -- you used a number of terms which I'd like for you to explain. But in terms of making these comparisons, is there an objective means by which that is done? In other words, is that independent of your experience or your judgement, or is that something that's related necessarily to that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: The -- producing the descriptions, the constructions, to a certain extent that is an objective process. The determining the significance of the features is a subjective process depending on the experience, because you need to be able to know how common or uncommon something is to know whether its significant, a difference or a similarity is significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned, for example, the notion of a range, or range of variation or variability, I guess, in an individual's writing. How do you go about assessing that, for example? Is that something that's derived from the specimen or is that something derived from the actual sample that you're -- that you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It's done from both. So you have to look at the range of variation within specimen writing and the range of variation within the questioned writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is there a certain norm within which one form of a writing, for example, is acceptable as falling within a range or outside of a range? Is there a certain number of characters, for example, that you look for that have similarities or differences in order to make that determination?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: You're looking at what -- you're comparing what you've got. So we don't have a set number of characters to look at. So we would look -- if we had sufficient writing, we would look at all the characters there, determine the range for those characters, and then compare the characters from one set of writing into the other to determine the similarities and the differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You also mention something called the "slant." And I'm quite a layperson but does that relate to the angle, so to speak, that the writing is taking place in?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It does. Some people have a very upright writing, some people slant forwards, some people slant backwards, some people are more variable. It's just one other aspect of a writing that we take into account when we are doing our comparisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how are you able to distinguish the slant of a writing, for example, from say, the angle of the paper that the person was writing on?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Because there'd still be a base-line that you would be comparing the angle against.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned the height of the writing, or I guess the ascension, you said, and the amount or the distance that it travels beneath a line, for example, of writing. And is that something that's -- well, that's something that you analyse clearly, but is that something that's quantifiable? Is that something that you measure in making a determination on the question of identity?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No, it's not a direct measure. It's just, again, another aspect of somebody's writing that you're looking at. Some people might do very large writing, some people do very small writing. Again, that's something you're looking at because you would like, with sufficient questioned specimen writing, to be able to match the two in their totality, so you would need to assess all the features to be able to determine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You also mentioned a concept -- or the concept of fluency or fluidity. Can you tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Fluency is related to the speed with which somebody can write. And it's how you get smooth curves, variation in pen pressure, the way the pen moves across the paper. Some people tend to be more skilled and will write much more fluently. Then people who are less used to writing tend to write more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, the type of work that you've done, aside from the work that you've done for the Office of the Prosecutor, does it involve or has it involved, I should say, for example, forgery or issues concerning forged documents, particularly signatures?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are there particular features of signatures that can tell you whether or not something is forged or attempted to have been forged or copied?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Generally, when somebody has to forge a signature, they have to make it look like the genuine signature because normally there is a genuine signature available for comparison. And so there are two aspects of the signature that have to match. The forger has to be able to get the pictorial appearance right because that's what people are expecting to see from that signature, but they also have to be able to get the fluency with which the person writes the signature correct. And generally we find that forgers can do one and not the other. So in an attempt to make something match pictorially, to look the same, obviously it's not their signature, they have to concentrate on the writing, that act of concentrating on the writing will slow it to down, so the fluency won't be as good. By contrast, to go back, that tends to be what people would do in forgeries. Most forgeries we see look like that. The other way is some people will decide it's a very fluent signature, possibly without a great deal of construction within it, and so they will attempt to produce something that looks fluent and be less worried that the actual way the pen has moved across the paper is the same between the two signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In reference to one of your reports, you refer to the notion of pictorial similarity in evaluating signature and which you've just talked about. You also mention something called pen lifts or unexpected pen lifts. Can you tell us what that means or what that involves?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Again it goes back to the concept of having to reproduce somebody else's signature. You have to really concentrate on it and often you have to stop and think half way through the signature where you're going to go to next to make it look similarly. So what we're talking about, pen lifts, is where somebody lifts the pen at a different point to where the genuine signature would -- signatory would lift their pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You also made reference to guide-lines with respect to signature analysis. Can you tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Again, depending on the circumstances in which the forgery is going to occur, if people -- if it's not going to be done in front of somebody, then there's an opportunity, possibly, to produce a guide-line so you could try and trace or in some other way produce a guide that you will then ink in, so you would be looking for guide-lines that somebody had gone over in producing a forged signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that something you can tell simply by examining the document where the signature is in terms of maybe the pressure with which its written or in terms of the consistency of the ink?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: You would be looking for possibly pencil lines or indentations associated with the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in one of your reports you also refer to the term asynchronous writing or synchronous writing. Can you tell us what that means just conceptually?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I think that -- it isn't -- they're not terms that I would use. I think I used them in reply to another expert's report. And I think the concept in which he was using them is that synchronous writing is one produced at one time, and asynchronous writing would be, for example, entries on a sheet of paper -- a number of entries on a sheet of paper that were produced at different times.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in your experience is it possible to determine the interval of time between a writing that was made and then another writing that -- or asynchronous writing that follows it?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Not generally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is there a difference between the idea of synchronous or asynchronous writing and contemporaneity in writing that you can examine? In other words, can you see the difference between writing that has been deposited on a piece of paper a significant period of time after the writing that you're examining? Or can you not tell the difference between the two in terms of the time-frame?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I think it would depend. You would be looking at various factors, for example, the use of different inks that could indicate things were -- may indicate that things were entered at a different time, not necessarily. You would also, I think, from the reading that I've done and the research that has been done on being able to identify this, I think what it boils down to is that you get much more consistency if you write one block of, say, one A4 sheet all in one go. It will visually have a much more consistent appearance than if you produce lots of separate entries on that sheet of paper on different -- at different times. The caveat with that would be is you would have to be able to know how consistent that writer was anyway, so you would need to be really certain that it -- of the difference between the two. You would need to know how they would habitually write. So you would need to have known samples of asynchronous writing and known samples of synchronous writing to be able to see how they actually make a difference within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: To put it another way, is it possible to determine, based upon a change, for example, within the range of variability of handwriting on a page from one section of an entry to another, is it possible to extrapolate from that how far apart these entries might have been made?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. It could be that you wrote a bit and somebody interrupted you, you took a phone call, you got up and stretched, sat back down again, and then continued it. That gap could be any length of time, and I don't think it would be possible to determine how big a gap, whether that was minutes or hours or days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would it be possible to make a determination as to when entries are made on a given piece of paper by analysing the age of the ink, the age of the ink relative to each writing?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It is possible if you have the same ink and the same piece of paper stored under the same conditions. There are -- it's not something that we would do. There are document examiners that do it to date but under very defined conditions because generally inks are dated by how they've dried, how the different components have changed over time. And that, there's a great deal of variability on that depending on how a document's been stored. Because obviously a document stored in sealed conditions versus one that's stored in direct sunlight, they will age differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is possible to make a determination as to the age of a given writing within a certain range? For example, you could tell -- can you tell the difference between writing that was made yesterday versus writing that was made 15 years ago versus writing that was made 150 years ago?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It is probably possible, depending on the inks that were used and the variation, that you could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would it be possible to make an analysis or determination as to when or how old the ink is relative to a deposit of ink or different deposits of ink that were within the same year, say 15 years ago or 20 years ago?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Within the same year, I doubt it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see that we've got two minutes before the break or so. I think I'm going to go to a different area, so I think now might be a good time to take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And before we break, I have to confess, you have been right with the 65 ter exhibit list. The three reports, the handwriting reports, 65 ter 2858, -59, and, -60 have already been on the 65 ter be exhibit list. I was told in the meantime. Please don't put these reports twice, this list now. We should have the next break now. And we will resume in half an hour, a quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, just before I call up the next exhibit, I wanted to ask you: In terms of expressing the results that you've reached in your reports, you used this scale, I think it's a 7-point scale, I wonder if you could just explain that to the Trial Chamber, how these gradations are made?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: How they're made or what they mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Both. Unfortunately, unlike certain areas of forensic science where there is a good body of statistics to be able to express statistically the strength of evidence, in handwriting there isn't, mainly because of the difficulties in isolating characters often and the interconnectivity of handwriting. So it isn't possible to come up with numbers to be able to assign to our strength of opinion. So, in common with all document examiners, we use a verbal scale. I think as you said before, at the top of the scale we would say conclusive evidence, either for or against, either the same person wrote it. Or conclusive evidence that the two pieces of writing were written by different people. And we would say that meant we could exclude the possibility of another person being responsible. Also in the middle, we have inconclusive, by which we can't tell one way or the other who's produced the writing. Between those two, we have two other points: Limited evidence; generally this means in fact there are similarities such that the person could have produced that writing, they are within pool of people that could have produced that writing, but for whatever reason you couldn't be more certain. It could be it was a very simple writing style with few distinctive features. It could be that the questioned writing was quite small in amount so you couldn't see all the characters. So while there were similarities, you wouldn't be able to be any stronger. And then between limited and conclusive we would have a scale of strong evidence in which case in one way there were similarities, there would be a lot of similarities, but it would just fall short of certainty. And so we would say there was strong evidence that the person had -- same people -- that person had written it and unlikely to be anybody else. But, again, for whatever reason, it could be you didn't have all the characters or there was a difference that you couldn't explain, you couldn't -- it would fall short of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that explanation. And what I'd like to show you is your report from 16 July 2003. And this relates to an analysis you did concerning Dragan Jokic. Do you have a copy of that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could have that in e-court, please. It's P1187.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Do you recognise it up here on this screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. What I'd like to do is to go to paragraph 5.3. That will be on page -- it should be page 4 in the English in e-court. Great. I think we have it also on the B/C/S. And in particular what I wanted to do was to just refer you to this paragraph and go over some of the findings that you've made. In this analysis, you concluded that certain entries in the duty officer's log-book appear to be those made by Dragan Jokic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you found in particular that it was strong evidence that the entries had been made by him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You also found that there was not conclusive evidence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And that is in relation to the findings expressed in 5.3 which concern, on page 0293-5744, the last six lines of that page?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I wanted to do is just to show you a couple of pages from the notebook itself. So you can keep that there in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what I'd like to do is to bring up P1459, please. Just so that the Court is aware, Mr. President, this is the -- what we call the teacher's edition or teacher's version of P14 which is the duty officer's notebook, and they're both in evidence. All right. I think we'll have to go to page 40 in the English. And if -- 40 in the B/C/S. If we could, because this has both the English and the B/C/S, if we could display side by side pages 40 and 41, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I think we've got it now on the screen. And per your findings in paragraph 5.3 of your report, that's P1187, the July 16th, 2003 report, you indicated that the last six lines from Muso Mani [phoen], excludeing the pencilled date and the name, bear strong evidence of having been written by Dragan Jokic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think that on the right-hand side of the screen we can't see all entries. Yes, that's better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you recall from the -- can you recall what specifically you were able to identify that showed that there was a confluence as it were, an overlap, between the entries from Muso Mani on the last six lines down through the bottom of the page in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There appears to be a difference in the ink that's used, or a difference in the colour of the ink. Can you see that one your --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You might not be able to see it, actually, on that screen.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It might help if you could stand a little bit just to look down on it, because I think the angle of the screen is a bit odd.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: They look different. They have a visual difference. And I think the bottom three lines are written -- are larger than the three above.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I think what I've said, actually, is that I've actually grouped the writings together, so it's taking the totality of what I've said with those questioned entries. So, for example, the A in both is constructed in the same way and is a much more unusual construction than you would get -- that you see in other writers in these books, for instance. But it's looking at the writing in its totality. It's the construction of all the characters that you can match.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So these two entries that we can see, that are basically split by the date in this page, as it is translated, "crush Muslims at Velja Glava and move towards Drina." And it says, "Mladenovac and Zljebac." And then you see the date 14/07. And then it says, "Colonel Salapura called Drago and Beara are to report to Golic." Per your conclusion, is this written by Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Strong evidence that it was written by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Strong evidence.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to go to another entry. And this we'll find at pages 44 and 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could display them also side by side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question at this point in time just in relation to this document on the screen. You say there's strong evidence that it was written Dragan Jokic. Which other material was available for you in comparing this handwritten -- Please let us go back to the previous page. I was putting a question to the previous pages. What other written material by Mr. Jokic was available for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Looking at my report, I was given a personal information form and I was told that there were certain entries in the operational diary that were written by Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What kind of personal information form are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've got the number. I can check in my file what it was. But I've got the ERN number. Would that help?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just in principle I would like to know which kind of material did you have at hand to compare with the entry in this notebook? Take your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The form that I've called the personal information form was one that looks to be a document from the Tribunal that had got Mr. Jokic's name, father's name, mother's name, date of birth, place of birth, his address, and his occupation. So I used that. And that was completed in 2001. And I was also told that there were certain entries that were his writing from the operational diary, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To explain the operational diary bit further? Mr. Vanderpuye can't help you at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He can't help you. He is not testifying; you are testifying. And I would like to get your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can tell you that all of the references that she used are documented in the reports, and there are three of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm convinced that this is the case, and hopefully we'll find all of that in the report. But I just put the question to the witness: Which kind of information and who provided you with this different handwriting documents? Are they from personal files of these people from the Republika Srpska or from Bosnia-Herzegovina or Republic of Serbia? Where did you get it from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was given it by the Office of the Prosecutor. I've called it "operational diary." It's got a 0076 number, which might be the IKM one. So I was given a personal information form that had obviously been completed from the Tribunal and I was told that there were certain entries from what I've described, I was obviously told at the time, was an operational diary that the Office of the Prosecutor were told were produced by Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think we were looking at the next entry, which was page 44 and 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this entry, this is ERN 0293-5746, you'll see that also in paragraph 5.3 of your report, you've indicated that all of the writing here, that there's strong evidence that this was made by Dragan Jokic as well?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And that's in comparing it to the preceding page that we've looked at and other material?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: That's comparing all the questioned writing together, to group it all together, and then comparing that grouped questioned writing with the specimen writing of Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And in this page we see here, particularly at 1500, and entrance that "Colonel Beara is coming in order to Orovoc, Petkovci, Rocevici, and Pilica," among other things, and you've discerned no significant difference between the entries that are indicated on this page.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to the next entry which we'll find at pages 44 and 55 -- 54 and 55. And this is ERN 0293-5751. Also you see that referenced in your report. And you've indicated that all of the writing on this page as well is -- there's strong evidence that it is of Dragan Jokic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in the middle of the page we see here an entry saying, "Beara to call 155." You see that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of both the letters and the numbers, you've found those to be consistent with Dragan Jokic's writing; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you the last one, which is at 56 and 57. And this corresponds to the next entry in paragraph 5.3 of your report. And here you also found that all of the writing was of Dragan Jokic. In particular, here you can see an entry at the top of the page, just above the number, the ERN number in the B/C/S version, you'll see it says, "od Beare."

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. The translation of that is, "from Beara," "Drago to report." And then it says, "Mane Djukic." And then it reads, "0900 Beara is coming." You see that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And both the numbers and the letters in this page you said are consistent with -- or rather I should say there's strong evidence that it's written by Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. It's part of the group of questioned writing that I've said there's strong evidence was written by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is there anything in particular concerning -- and I'm just saying this as a layperson, but I see slanted writing in the middle of the page there; can you see that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then I can also see capital letters and small-case letters.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us how you arrived at the conclusion that this was within, say, the normal range of variation for a single writer, in particular Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Because we're looking at not just -- those are some features of the slant, but primarily we're actually looking at some -- the construction of the characters, how the pen's moved across the paper to create those individual characters. And so in these cases all those entries bear the same construction of the characters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. I want to take you to a different area, if I could. I'd like to show you your report. Just bear with me one moment. I just want to go over your new reports with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to have in e-court, please, 65 ter 2860. That's a 16 August 2007 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You may have it on the screen in front of you. Do you recognise the report first?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can just go on to the first page or so. I think we'll have to go to the following page. There we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you see the "purpose of the examination"?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall being -- do you recall this report in particular?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It's not one of the ones that I've actually got the case file for.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, if I could just take you to paragraph -- first let me just read into the record what we have here. The purpose of the examination, you've indicated here, was to determine whether or not there is any evidence that Dragan Jokic wrote any of the entries for 18 July in the duty officer notebook. And you concluded here that there were -- there is conclusive evidence - and that's at paragraph 5.4, page 5 in English - that Dragan Jokic produced the writings for the entries listed in paragraph 3 which correspond to pages 0293-5777 and 5778 in the duty officer's log-book. Now, at the time that you produced the report - I can see that you've signed it - would you say that you still subscribe to the findings that you've made?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would offer this report into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you please give me the number again, the 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's 2860, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1967, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you, also, 65 ter 2858, which is a 1st August, 2008, report. And if we go to paragraph number 3, I think it's page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You see here also the purpose that the documents were provided and then, of course, the purpose of the examination, which in this case was whether or not there's any evidence that any of the user's signatures or the officer's signatures on the vehicle logs were produced by Drago Nikolic. Do you recall this report?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we go to page 5 of this report, we can see your conclusions. It's under item 6.6 and 6.7. And under item 6.6, you say: "In my opinion, there's conclusive evidence that Drago Nikolic produced the specified signatures on the vehicle log ERN 0069-4704." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And further, in paragraph 6.7, you indicate that in your opinion there are certain similarities in the documents in the entries listed above, those relating to 14th of July, 1995, 16th of July, 1995, and so on, which provide limited evidence that Drago Nikolic produced the specified signatures in vehicle log 0069-4702. You see that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you subscribe -- continue to subscribe to the findings you made in this report?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would move this report into evidence as well. Its 65 ter 2858.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This will be received too.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1968, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you 65 ter 2859, please. All right. I think we've got it up on the screen now. And if I could, I'd like to take you to page number 3 of this document, item number 3 and 4. It will be -- it will go over also into the next page in the B/C/S. But the items here that you've provided were a vehicle log -- two vehicle logs and some other documents that are listed in number 3, and the purpose of this examination was to determine if there was any evidence that the user's signatures or the entries dated 19 July and 23 July on vehicle log ERN 44 -- 0447-0889 through 0890 were produced by Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to your conclusions here in paragraph 6.5 on page 5 in the English. I think we have it in the B/C/S also. And what you wrote here was that "the questioned signatures are fluently written and do not show any of the features commonly associated with simulated signatures such as guide-lines or unexpected pen lifts." And you go on to conclude that in your opinion, "the similarities provide strong evidence that Vujadin Popovic produced the signatures for the entries dated 19 and 23 July." Do you stand by those findings?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would move 65 ter 2859 into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This will be received as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1969, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to show you now, just bear with me for one moment, is P157. This is the vehicle log that is referred to in your report. And if we go to the next page in the B/C/S and the English, I guess, we'll find the entries for the 19th and 23rd of July. You can see that the first two entries on the left are for the 19th of July. And if we scroll over to the right, we can see the signatures that we're talking about. Okay. Now, just based on this, what you have in front of you -- are you able to see that, first of all, on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you recognise the signatures that you identified as being consistent with Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It's the first two that are in blue, the lighter blue. And then the next -- then there's two that weren't. And the next set of three.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And if we go back over to the left-hand side, we can see the corresponding dates of entry. And here we see the first two are for 19 July, the next two are for the 20th and 21st of July, and then the following three are for the 23rd of July as you identified in your report. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you some of the reference signatures that you used for comparison. If I could show you first 65 ter 189.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is a Drina Corps security department document dated 15 April 1995 concerning the arrest and detention of POWs and reporting a telegram from the security administration of the VRS. And if we go to the next page -- I'm sorry, to the third page in the B/C/S, we'll find our signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall this as being one of the documents you used as a reference sample concerning the identification that you made of Popovic's signature in the vehicle log?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't know if it's possible, but maybe we can display side by side the reference page which is ERN 0447-0890, and that's in P157. It should be page number 2. I'm reminded, we also -- we don't need the English up on the screen. We can do without it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, are you able to describe some of the similarities that you relied on in order to make the identification in terms of the height or the slant or the fluidity of the signature, if you're able?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It's more -- I think -- I've tried to explain. It's not just a one-against-one comparison. So obviously I had more than one specimen signature to take into account here. So it's not just -- I'm not going to able to match everything in this one specimen. Also, judging from the copies I've got, it's not come out particularly clearly. The stamp's obscured quite a lot of the detail on this one, so what we've been looking for is that actually the pen path is -- its quite complicated. I think, especially without looking at it with a microscope and taking a bit of time to work out exactly how the signature is being constructed, it would be very difficult for somebody to just come along and reproduce the same pen path, which is what the case is here. So the way the pen has moved across the paper to form the signatures is the same in both. We're also looking at the flourish that you get across it, again, which is similar in the two of them. That would probably the main things in these. These are particularly difficult to be able to illustrate it. A, because the specimen signature is quite dark you can't see much of the detail, especially of the first part. And because of the size of the boxes for the questioned ones, there's a lot of overlapping going on. But from my examination, the pen path is the same in both. And the fluidity, the fluency is the same. You can see from the questioned signatures, I think even from the image on the screen, that there's a variation in pen pressure. The blue changes colour which is an indication of fluency. Because if you're trying to copy that, you would have to write much more slowly to ensure that you've got a good match, in which case the pen tends to leave an even track. Whereas when you're writing your own signature, you know when you're suddenly going to -- when you're going to take the pen off, so in effect you're starting to move the pen off as it's coming up to a break or a change of direction so that you get that variation pressure which you can see on there. So, again, they're very fluently written, and it's a very complex signature to be able to reproduce.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is this one of the documents that you relied on, though, in making your analysis?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It's one of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document on the left side of the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: 65 ter number 00189.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1970, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you one more document in respect of this particular report, and that's 65 ter 2205.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a document that's also from the Drina Corps. It's indicating from the intelligence and security department dated 18 July 1995. And this one deals with or concerns dealing with reporter crews. If we go to -- we have it all right down there -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If we can display this side by side against the document we had previously up there at P157, page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that you only need the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Only the B/C/S. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: While that's coming up, can you identify this as a document that you relied on in respect of your report as well?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It was one of the specimen signatures that I was provided with, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The left one, please, enlarged on the signature block. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you -- first of all, did you examine the originals of these documents that I'm showing you?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that relates to the documents I showed you previously concerning having -- bearing Colonel Popovic's signature?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And with respect to this document, did you make the same kind of assessment as you've previously described in comparing it to this vehicle log, that is, a microscopic analysis of it or an analysis of it in a way that you were able to -- were you able to see, for example, beyond the stamp of it and that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. Again, the original, it's easier to see where it is over the stamp, but, again, it's not just this one signature. You're looking at all the specimen signatures to determine the range of variation, that they are all fit together as specimens. So what you're looking for is how he reproduces his signature on different occasions, so hence the reason this one is slightly different to the previous one we saw. But again it just expands that range of variation that you're seeing, that you would wish the questioned signatures to fit into.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with that I would also tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have one more report to go through. I see that we are at the end of our time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 2205 will become Exhibit P1971.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must come to an end, but you should try to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have about 15 or 20 minutes more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is very unsatisfactory. Your indication was one hour with this witness, and you used more than one hour up to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, I thought my estimate had been an hour and a half. Maybe I'm mistaken. But in any event, you're right; I would have exceeded my time certainly if I continue into tomorrow, which I would like to do, to address this last issue, but I think I've used up just about an hour and a half. An hour and 15 minutes, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your estimation was one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I apologise, it should have been an hour and a half, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We can't continue now. You should continue your examination-in-chief and consider during the break how to shorten the examination-in-chief as much as possible. We have to adjourn for the day. We resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
